system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 6 — Jazz Standard Study #5: Sweet Georgia Brown

_Pages 87-101._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## VI7 dominant substitution rule

> Sweet Georgia Brown starts on the VI7. |t wouldn’t seem like such a
> surprising way to start if it was a minor 7 chord (meaning it would be
> the relative minor). However, the vi minor is converted into a VI domi-
> nant.

**Significance (p. 94).** This passage defines the core harmonic rule at work in the song -- that diatonic minor chords can be raised to dominant 7ths -- which recurs throughout the chapter's analysis.

## Converting minor chords to dominant 7ths

> just
> know that it is entirely normal and acceptable to turn minor chords in
> the diatonic series into dominant 7“ chords.

**Significance (p. 95).** This is the explicit rule stated for when and why chord quality can be altered within a diatonic progression, making it the generalisable takeaway beyond this one song.

## Cycle of dominant 7ths in 4ths

> bars 1-13 are just a long cycle of dominant 7* chords resolving to the |
> chord.

**Significance (p. 95).** This concise analytical summary frames how to hear and navigate the entire A-section, giving the student a single structural handle for the most harmonically dense passage.

## Relative minor key transition

> Starting in the second half of bar 24 we begin to transition into the
> relative minor key. What's the relative minor to Ab major? F minor.

**Significance (p. 96).** Pinpointing the exact bar of the key-center shift to the relative minor teaches students to hear and mark harmonic pivots in real time.

## Descending chromatic dominant approach

> Don't let this section throw you either. Understand we are just dealing
> with a series of chromatically descending dominant 7“ chords that are
> targeting the VI7 chord. From there the VI7 logically concludes to a ii-
> V-| to the parent tonic.

**Significance (p. 97).** This is the rule for understanding and demystifying the chromatic tail section of the song -- recognising it as a directed approach to the VI7 rather than arbitrary chromaticism.

## Backdoor I7-VI7-ii-V-I label

> You can simplify your understanding of this section by noting that it
> starts on the I7 and is targeting the VI7. You can think of bars 29-32
> as a “backdoor” |7-VI7-ii-V-I.

**Significance (p. 97).** This names a reusable analytical shorthand -- 'backdoor' -- that students can apply to similar chromatic dominant sequences in other standards.

## Mixolydian scale definition

> The easiest way to think of a Mixolydian scale is a major scale with a
> b7. Or you can think of it as starting and ending a major scale on its
> 5* tone.
>
> Formula: 1-2-3-4-5-6-b7

**Significance (p. 99).** This is the chapter's central scale definition, providing two complementary mental models plus a formula that the student will use directly for improvisation over dominant 7 chords.

## Scales as pitch collections

> best way to think about the use of scales is “pitch collections.” They
> aren’t notes that are meant to be played in order, nor are they to be
> used solely to improvise. They are simply pitch collections which map
> out the note choices you can use to make melodies over a particular
> chord.

**Significance (p. 99).** This reframes the pedagogical purpose of scales from mechanical running to melodic resource, which is a fundamental conceptual shift for improvisation students.

## Mixolydian chord-tone pattern exercise

> Note that each bar starts on a different chord tone of the given chord.
> The first and last lines begin with quarter note chord tones moving in
> ascending order: R-3'*-5*-b7. The second line descends in this order:
> R-b7-5°%-3°¢.

**Significance (p. 100).** This specifies the exact finger/pitch pattern of the foundational exercise, giving students a concrete melodic template that maps Mixolydian note choices onto the cycling dominant changes.

## Licks at micro level vs. macro composition

> In past improv lessons we have looked at composing music on a macro
> level, but licks are great for breaking things down to a micro level.

**Significance (p. 101).** This defines the pedagogical role of licks within the method's broader improvisation curriculum, clarifying when and why to practice isolated phrases versus full-chorus composition.

## Transposing licks through all 12 keys

> | always suggest taking things through all 12 keys. It’s a powerful
> practice that not only helps you internalize musical information, but it
> also enables you to become stronger in keys you may be weaker at.

**Significance (p. 101).** This is the method's explicit rule for how to practice any short musical phrase, making key-transposition a non-negotiable part of the lick-learning workflow.
